title: Pinocchio is robbed of his gold coins, and as punishment gets four months in prison.
paragraphs: The puppet returned to town and began counting the minutes one by one: and when he thought it was time, he immediately took the road back to the Field of Miracles.
And as he hurried along, his heart beat hard, going tick, tock, tick, tock, like a grandfather clock when it is really racing. And meanwhile he thought to himself:

“And what if, instead of a thousand coins, I found two thousand on the tree’s branches? And what if, instead of two thousand, I found five thousand? And what if, instead of five thousand, I found a hundred thousand? What a fine gentleman I would become! I’d like a beautiful palace, a thousand little wooden horses and a thousand stables to play with, a cellar full of sweet rose liqueur and red spice liqueur, and a bookcase full of candied fruit, cakes, sweet fruit breads, almond sweets and rolled wafers with cream.”

Dreaming like this, he came near the field and stopped to see whether he could spot a tree with branches loaded with coins: but he saw nothing. He took another hundred steps, and nothing; he entered the field… went right up to the little hole where he had buried his gold coins, and nothing. Then he grew worried and, forgetting the rules of manners and good behaviour, took a hand out of his pocket and gave his head a very long scratch.
Just then he heard a loud laugh ringing in his ears: and looking up, he saw a large parrot in a tree, picking pests out of the few feathers it had left.
“Why are you laughing?” Pinocchio asked crossly.
“I’m laughing because while cleaning my feathers, I tickled myself under my wings.”
The puppet did not answer. He went to the water channel and, filling the same slipper with water, began watering the earth covering the gold coins again.
Then another laugh, even ruder than the first, rang out in the quiet emptiness of the field.
“Now then,” shouted Pinocchio, growing angry, “will you tell me, you rude Parrot, what you’re laughing at?”
“I’m laughing at those fools who believe every bit of nonsense and let themselves be trapped by anyone cleverer than they are.”
“Are you talking about me?”

“Yes, I’m talking about you, poor Pinocchio: you, who are silly enough to believe that money can be planted and harvested in fields, just like beans and pumpkins. I believed it once too, and today I’m paying for it. Today, though too late, I’ve had to accept that to put together a little money honestly, you must know how to earn it, either by working with your own hands or by using your own head.”
“I don’t understand you,” said the puppet, who was already beginning to tremble with fear.

“Oh well! I’ll explain more clearly,” added the Parrot. “You see, while you were in town, the Fox and the Cat came back to this field: they took the buried gold coins, and then ran away like the wind. And now, good luck to anyone trying to catch them!”

Pinocchio’s mouth fell open, and, refusing to believe the Parrot’s words, he began digging with his hands and nails in the ground he had watered. And digging, digging, digging, he made a hole so deep that a haystack could have fitted into it upright: but the coins were gone.
Then, filled with despair, he ran back to town and went straight to the courthouse to report the two scoundrels who had robbed him to the judge.

The judge was a large ape of the gorilla family: an old ape respected for his great age, his white beard and especially his golden glasses, without lenses, which he had to wear all the time because of sore, watering eyes that had troubled him for several years.

Standing before the judge, Pinocchio told every detail of the wicked trick that had been played on him; he gave the names, surnames and descriptions of the scoundrels, and ended by asking for justice.
The judge listened very kindly; he took a great interest in the story: his heart softened, and he was moved: and when the puppet had nothing more to say, he reached out his hand and rang a bell.
At the sound of the bell, two mastiff dogs dressed as policemen appeared at once.
Then the judge pointed Pinocchio out to the policemen and said:
“That poor fellow has been robbed of four gold coins: so take him and put him in prison at once.”
The puppet, hearing this sentence fall on him out of nowhere, was stunned and wanted to protest: but the policemen, to avoid wasting time, covered his mouth and took him to jail.

And there he had to stay for four months: four very long months: and he would have stayed even longer, if something very lucky had not happened. For you should know that the young Emperor who ruled the town of Foolcatcher, having won a great victory over his enemies, ordered big public celebrations, lights, fireworks, horse races and bicycle races, and, as an extra sign of joy, ordered the prisons opened and all the criminals let out.
“If the others are getting out of prison, I want to get out too,” Pinocchio said to the jailer.
“Not you,” replied the jailer, “because you’re not one of that fine crowd…”
“I beg your pardon,” replied Pinocchio, “I’m a criminal too.”
“In that case you’re quite right,” said the jailer; and taking off his cap respectfully and bowing to him, he opened the prison doors and let him go.
